title: Microsoft’s “Clea” Maia 300 Inference XPU Is A Bandwidth Beast
gist: Microsoft's Maia 300 'Clea' inference XPU (TSMC N2P chiplet package, 288 GB HBM4) is claimed to deliver up to 7X rack-level token throughput and 2.5X perf/watt over Maia 200, with a 12,288-accelerator coherency domain. Morgan reads it as inference-first design that drops full memory coherence, mirroring OpenAI's 'Jalapeno'.

insights.claim: Microsoft claims a 96-XPU Maia 300 rack delivers up to 7X the token throughput of a 48-XPU Maia 200 rack, at 2.5X better performance per watt; only about 36% more flops per chip and 2X XPU count explain part of it, so the rest must come from architecture and dataflow.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Efficiency (perf/W) rather than raw flops is the claimed gain; if real it lowers Microsoft's cost per token and reliance on Nvidia for inference.
insights.quote: Here is the metric that Microsoft is likely most proud of: You get that 7X performance improvement with a 2.5X improvement in performance per watt.
insights.locator: These are raw feeds and speeds

insights.claim: The Maia 300 is designed for effective real-world GenAI inference performance rather than spec-sheet flops, with larger agentic workloads of dozens to hundreds of models sharing network and memory space at low latency as the target.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Agentic multi-model workloads are now shaping silicon design; watch whether inference ASIC specs shift toward memory/network over compute.
insights.locator: The Maia 300 chip is a much-improved device

insights.claim: Raw per-chip specs are modest relative to rack gains: a Maia 300 gets only 36% more flops than Maia 200, so the 7X rack figure leans heavily on doubling XPUs per rack and unexplained dataflow improvements.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Treat the 7X claim as vendor-stated and unverified until the technical paper appears; Morgan expects it about a year out.
insights.locator: These are raw feeds and speeds

themes.theme: Microsoft Maia program scale and deployment

insights.claim: Microsoft says Maia 200 now runs inference for Copilot and helps develop new models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry moving to Maia 200 by year end; it will serve OpenAI, Microsoft and open-source models, though how much of OpenAI's GPT API runs on Maia is unclear.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Captive inference demand from Copilot/OpenAI gives the custom-silicon program a volume base that reduces GPU purchases at the margin.
insights.locator: In a separate announcement by Scott Guthrie

insights.claim: Rumor says Microsoft wants at least 1 million Maia sockets in the field; at 1.74 kW per accelerator, a gigawatt is about 575,000 Maia 300 devices, and Guthrie promised 'multi-gigawatt deployments' on Azure.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Multi-GW Maia plans translate into substantial TSMC N2, HBM4 and Ethernet switch demand outside Nvidia.
insights.locator: The rumor mill is that Microsoft wants

insights.claim: Microsoft has iterated Maia over three generations (Maia 100 in November 2023, Maia 200 in January 2026, Maia 300 now) and Morgan notes it often gets chips right on the second or third try, with Maia 200 ramping on Azure this year.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cadence of roughly annual new generations suggests a durable in-house roadmap, not an experiment.
insights.locator: Microsoft is no slouch when it comes to designing chips

insights.claim: Chip design partner for Maia 300 is not disclosed; Global UniChip was shepherd for Maia 100 and is presumed for later parts, while rumors linked Marvell and Broadcom to Microsoft custom silicon, and Arm now selling its own processor may change the CPU shepherd.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Custom-ASIC design-services share (GUC vs Broadcom vs Marvell) at Microsoft is an open competitive question.
insights.locator: Microsoft has not said who its chip shepherd

insights.claim: Maia 300 moves from monolithic reticle-limit dies to a chiplet package on TSMC N2P: seven chips and eight HBM4 stacks on an interposer, 288 GB HBM4 at 18 TB/sec, with I/O and HBM controllers split from compute and SRAM.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Another hyperscaler adopting N2-class plus advanced packaging adds to leading-edge and CoWoS-type capacity tightness.
insights.locator: With the Clea XPU, Microsoft is moving to the 2 nanometer

insights.claim: Morgan estimates the Clea package at about 1,980 mm2 (2.4X Braga's 810 mm2) and roughly 280 billion transistors excluding HBM, and guesses I/O dies use 5 nm because shrinking I/O raises cost and cuts yield without improving performance; these are his estimates, not Microsoft disclosures.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Estimates only; size implies large packaging and cost per unit.
insights.locator: As for area and transistor count

insights.claim: Maia 300 ties pairs of compute tiles to pairs of HBM4 banks in a NUMA-like way rather than sharing all HBM across all tiles as Maia 200 did, and links only two accelerators tightly instead of four; OpenAI and Broadcom took the same tack in 'Jalapeno', and Morgan admits he over-values coherence.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Two hyperscaler designs converging on partitioned memory suggests inference prefers locality over full coherence, a hint at where Nvidia-style NVLink advantages matter less.
insights.quote: As I have been warned by some techies, I over-value coherence. Apparently Microsoft did, too.
insights.locator: With the Maia 300, a pair of compute tiles

insights.claim: Maia generations kept cutting on-chip SRAM relative to HBM in Maia 200 (more HBM capacity and bandwidth, less SRAM); Morgan guesses Maia 300 has about 400 MB SRAM in compute plus 200 MB in I/O chiplets and ~166 TB/sec aggregate SRAM bandwidth against 18 TB/sec HBM.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Bandwidth, not flops, is the bottleneck being engineered around for inference.

insights.claim: Moving from 2U to 1U servers with next-gen liquid cooling doubles Maia 300 to 96 XPUs per rack (about 167 kW), and across 128 racks gives a 12,288-accelerator single coherency domain over the ATL 2.0 Ethernet network.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Ethernet-based scale-up at this size benefits merchant Ethernet switch silicon vendors and liquid cooling suppliers.
insights.locator: Microsoft has a next generation of liquid cooling

insights.claim: The 12,288-device domain is the biggest coherency domain among the big cloud builders, versus 72 or 144 GPUs in Nvidia and AMD racks, 576 or 1,152 in promised multi-tier NVSwitch fabrics, 9,600 for Google's Sunfish TPU 8t and 1,152 for Zebrafish TPU 8i.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Scale-up domain size is becoming a competitive axis for agentic inference; compare against Nvidia roadmap claims.
insights.locator: That is the biggest coherency domain we have heard of yet

insights.claim: Maia's custom RoCE Ethernet (ATL) has scaled each generation: Maia 100 2,304 devices, Maia 200 6,144 devices with 2.3X bandwidth at 1.5X power, using 4-bit MXFP4 and 1.5X more cores to reach 3.4X the flops of Maia 100.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Microsoft is betting on Ethernet rather than proprietary NVLink-class fabrics for scale-up.
insights.locator: This Braga chip had much more HBM memory
